name: Harvard
description: Brandy, sweet vermouth and bitters with a splash of soda — a Manhattan built on cognac, and the oldest of the college cocktails.
funFact: Brandy was America's default spirit until phylloxera destroyed the French vineyards in the 1870s and whiskey took its place — most brandy cocktails date from before that shift.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Duplex
description: Both vermouths in equal measure with orange bitters. No base spirit at all, and a staple order before Prohibition.
funFact: Vermouth-only cocktails filled American afternoon drinking until Prohibition killed the habit; the category had to be rediscovered from books eighty years later.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Vermouth Cocktail
description: Sweet vermouth with bitters and a cherry, stirred cold. The simplest drink in the nineteenth-century canon.
funFact: Jerry Thomas lists it in 1862 with no base spirit — proof that a cocktail was originally defined by structure, spirit plus sugar plus bitters, rather than by strength.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Absinthe Frappé
description: Absinthe, anisette and mint shaken over crushed ice until the glass frosts white. New Orleans in the heat.
funFact: The Old Absinthe House on Bourbon Street has served it since the 1870s, and a song was written about it in 1904 — decades before absinthe was banned in America.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in a shaker.
Add the absinthe, anisette and crushed ice and shake hard until the tin frosts.
Pour unstrained into a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda and crown with mint.

name: Absinthe Suissesse
description: Absinthe with orgeat, cream and egg white, blended pale green. A New Orleans breakfast drink, and served as one.
funFact: It is served in the French Quarter as a morning drink, and Brennan's has poured it at breakfast for decades alongside eggs and turtle soup.

steps: Add all ingredients to a blender with crushed ice.
Blend until pale green, smooth and frothy.
Pour into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a mint sprig and serve immediately.

name: Roffignac
description: Cognac with raspberry shrub and soda over ice — named for a New Orleans mayor of the 1820s.
funFact: Count Louis Philippe de Roffignac was mayor of New Orleans from 1820 to 1828 and is credited with the city's first street lighting and paved roads.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the cognac and raspberry shrub and stir.
Top with cold soda water.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Alabazam
description: Cognac, curaçao, lemon and a heavy hand of Angostura. Named by a Victorian barman for no reason anyone recorded.
funFact: The bitters measure is unusually large for the era — a full two teaspoons where most recipes call for dashes, which is what gives the drink its name-worthy kick.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Fanciulli
description: A Manhattan with Fernet-Branca in place of the bitters. Minty, medicinal and considerably more assertive.
funFact: Fernet-Branca has been made in Milan since 1845 and contains around 27 botanicals; its recipe is held by the Branca family and has never been published.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Star Cocktail
description: Applejack and sweet vermouth with bitters — the apple-brandy Manhattan, and older than most whiskey ones.
funFact: Applejack was made in colonial America by freezing cider and removing the ice — a method called jacking, which is where the spirit gets its name.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Bombay Cocktail
description: Brandy, both vermouths, curaçao and absinthe. Five ingredients, all of them aromatic, and no citrus anywhere.
funFact: It has nothing to do with Bombay — interwar bar books attached imperial place names to drinks with no connection to them, which is most of the Savoy's geography.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Metropole
description: Brandy and dry vermouth with Peychaud's and orange bitters. The Metropolitan's drier twin, from the hotel of the same name.
funFact: The Hotel Metropole stood on Broadway and was notorious enough that gambler Herman Rosenthal was shot outside it in 1912, in a case that brought down a police lieutenant.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Metropolitan
description: Brandy and sweet vermouth with bitters and a little sugar. The sweeter half of a Victorian pair.
funFact: Not to be confused with the 1990s vodka-and-cranberry Metropolitan, which shares the name and nothing else — the collision is a century apart.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Third Rail
description: Rum, brandy and applejack in equal measure with an absinthe rinse. Named for the electrified rail, and appropriately.
funFact: Three base spirits at equal measure with no dilution beyond stirring — this is among the strongest drinks in the classic canon by design rather than accident.

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe and discard the excess.
Stir the rum, brandy and applejack over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into the rinsed coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and serve.

name: Honeymoon
description: Calvados, Bénédictine, curaçao and lemon — from a Berkshires restaurant, and one of the better applejack sours.
funFact: It comes from the Hotel Wentworth's Honeymoon Cocktail via a 1930s Massachusetts restaurant, and is sometimes printed as the Farmer's Daughter.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Bosom Caresser
description: Brandy, curaçao and grenadine shaken with a whole egg yolk. Rich, orange-red and named with Victorian directness.
funFact: Nineteenth-century drink names were startlingly frank — the Bosom Caresser sits in the same books as the Corpse Reviver and the Maiden's Blush.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate nutmeg over the surface.

name: Deauville
description: Calvados and cognac with Cointreau and lemon — a Sidecar split between grape and apple brandy.
funFact: Deauville on the Normandy coast was the fashionable summer resort of interwar Paris, close enough to the calvados orchards to explain the recipe.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Depth Bomb
description: Calvados and cognac with lemon and grenadine — a First World War name for a drink of apple and grape.
funFact: Depth charges were new technology in 1916, and the drink joined a wave of cocktails named after weapons that also gave us the Whizz Bang and the French 75.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Chicago Cocktail
description: Brandy and curaçao with bitters, topped with champagne in a sugar-rimmed glass.
funFact: The sugared rim is the tell of a whole family of nineteenth-century 'crusta'-influenced drinks, of which the Brandy Crusta is the best-known survivor.

steps: Rim a chilled coupe with lemon and caster sugar.
Shake the brandy, curaçao and bitters with ice.
Strain into the rimmed coupe.
Top slowly with champagne and serve.
recipe.garnish: A sugared rim and a lemon twist

name: Brandy Champarelle
description: Curaçao, yellow Chartreuse, anisette and brandy, layered in that order. A New Orleans pousse-café.
funFact: Layering works on sugar density: the sweetest liqueur goes first and the driest spirit last, which is why the brandy floats on top rather than sinking.

steps: Pour the curaçao into a pony glass.
Float the yellow Chartreuse over the back of a barspoon.
Float the anisette the same way, then the brandy last.
Serve immediately without stirring.
recipe.garnish: None — the layers are the presentation

name: Silver Fizz
description: A Gin Fizz with egg white shaken through it. The silver is the foam, and it is the whole difference.
funFact: The fizz family is graded by egg: silver takes the white, golden the yolk, and royal the whole egg — three named drinks from one recipe.

steps: Dry-shake everything except the soda without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water to lift the foam and serve at once.

name: Golden Fizz
description: A Gin Fizz built on the yolk instead of the white — richer, rounder and pale gold rather than white.
funFact: The yolk emulsifies rather than foams, so a Golden Fizz has body where a Silver Fizz has head — the same trick that separates a flip from a sour.

steps: Dry-shake everything except the soda without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water to lift the foam and serve at once.

name: Royal Fizz
description: The whole egg, white and yolk together. Foam and body at once, and the richest member of the family.
funFact: A whole egg needs a longer dry shake than either half alone — twenty seconds minimum, or the white and yolk never properly combine.

steps: Dry-shake everything except the soda without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Strain into a chilled glass with no ice.
Top slowly with soda water to lift the foam and serve at once.

name: Diamond Fizz
description: A Gin Fizz topped with champagne instead of soda. Also sold as a French 75 with the ratio moved.
funFact: The line between a Diamond Fizz and a French 75 is almost entirely a matter of which book you are reading and how much gin is in it.

steps: Shake the gin, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Strain into a chilled highball glass with no ice.
Top slowly with champagne.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and serve.

name: Gin Daisy
description: Gin, lemon and grenadine over crushed ice with a splash of soda. The daisy is the template the Margarita descends from.
funFact: Margarita is Spanish for daisy, and a Margarita is structurally a tequila daisy — spirit, citrus and a sweetener, served the same way.

steps: Shake the gin, lemon juice and grenadine hard with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a mint sprig.

name: Brandy Daisy
description: The daisy built on cognac, with yellow Chartreuse standing in for part of the sweetener.
funFact: Nineteenth-century books print the daisy separately for every base spirit — gin, brandy, whiskey, rum — as four entries rather than one recipe with a note.

steps: Shake the cognac, lemon juice, Chartreuse and grenadine with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.

name: Whiskey Daisy
description: Rye, lemon and grenadine over crushed ice. The American branch of the daisy family.
funFact: The daisy, the fix, the fizz and the cobbler are all the same idea at different dilutions — the nineteenth century organised drinks by structure rather than by base.

steps: Shake the rye, lemon juice and grenadine hard with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Top with a splash of soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and seasonal berries.

name: Gin Fix
description: Gin, lemon, sugar and a little water over crushed ice, fruit piled on top. A sour served long and cold.
funFact: A fix differs from a sour only in being built over crushed ice in the glass rather than shaken and strained — the fruit garnish is doing the work of the presentation.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the lemon juice and water in the glass.
Add the gin and stir once.
Fill with crushed ice and churn with a barspoon until frosted.
Cap with more crushed ice and pile fruit on top.
recipe.garnish: Seasonal fruit piled on the ice

name: Whiskey Fix
description: Bourbon over crushed ice with lemon and sugar, fruit heaped over. The fix, in its most-ordered form.
funFact: Crushed ice was a luxury before mechanical refrigeration — a fix or a julep was a display of a bar's ice supply as much as its bartending.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in the lemon juice and water in the glass.
Add the bourbon and stir.
Fill with crushed ice and churn until the glass frosts.
Top with more ice and heap fruit over it.
recipe.garnish: Seasonal fruit and a lemon wheel

name: Whiskey Cobbler
description: Bourbon over crushed ice with sugar and fruit, churned until frosted. The cobbler that made the straw famous.
funFact: The Sherry Cobbler popularised the drinking straw in the 1840s — before it, straws were literal rye stalks, and the cobbler is what made them a bar fixture.

steps: Muddle the orange slices with the sugar in a goblet.
Add the bourbon and fill with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the glass frosts.
Cap with more ice, heap the berries on top and add a straw.
recipe.garnish: Orange slices, berries and a mint sprig

name: Brandy Cobbler
description: Cognac, sugar and orange over crushed ice — the cobbler with brandy in place of sherry or whiskey.
funFact: Cobblers were among the first American drinks to reach Europe; Dickens wrote about encountering one on his 1842 American tour and being impressed by the straw.

steps: Muddle the orange with the sugar in a goblet.
Add the cognac and fill with crushed ice.
Churn until the outside of the glass frosts.
Top with more ice and pile fruit over it.

name: Whiskey Rickey
description: Bourbon, lime and soda with no sugar at all. The rickey's defining feature is what it leaves out.
funFact: The rickey was created for lobbyist Joe Rickey in Washington in the 1880s with whiskey; the gin version came later and took the name with it.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Squeeze half a lime in and drop the spent shell into the glass.
Add the bourbon and top with cold soda water.
Stir once and serve with no sugar — that is the point of a rickey.

name: Pierre Collins
description: The Collins built on cognac. Same lemon, sugar and soda; a rounder, fruitier result.
funFact: The Collins family names by base spirit — Tom for Old Tom gin, John for whiskey, Pierre for cognac, Pedro for rum, Mike for Irish whiskey.

steps: Shake the cognac, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

name: Pedro Collins
description: The rum Collins. Lighter than the whiskey version and sharper than the gin one.
funFact: Collins glasses are named after the drink rather than the other way round — the tall, narrow shape exists to keep a long soda drink carbonated.

steps: Shake the rum, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Garnish with a lemon wheel and a cherry.
recipe.garnish: A lemon wheel and a cherry

name: Bamboo Royale
description: The Bamboo lengthened with champagne — sherry and vermouth under bubbles, and lower proof than almost anything.
funFact: The Bamboo was created at Yokohama's Grand Hotel in the 1890s; adding champagne follows the French 'Royale' convention applied to a Japanese-invented drink.

steps: Stir the sherry, vermouth and bitters over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with champagne.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and serve.
